strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper systematically investigates the underexplored regime between SFT and RL, framed around whether RL with adaptive partial supervision can induce genuinely new reasoning capabilities rather than reweighting existing behavior.

The AdaBack algorithm is simple, elegant, and genuinely per-sample: the stochastic binary search over the supervision ratio using GRPO's group-level reward estimates removes the need for hand-crafted curriculum staging, which is a practical advantage over prior work like R3 and Salimans & Chen's backtracking.

The synthetic chain-of-parities task provides a clean separation result (AdaBack succeeds where SFT, RL, and SFT+RL all fail), backed by a plausible theoretical sketch connecting the curriculum to reduced parity degree and known SQ/SGD sample-complexity results for sparse parities.

Evaluation goes beyond standard benchmarks: the introduced Base-7 and Tensor-2 GSM8k variants are sensible probes of generalization beyond pretraining exposure and longer-horizon reasoning, and the pass@k analysis directly tests the increasingly important claim (contra Yue et al.) that the method expands the solution space rather than reweighting it.

The paper is honest about limitations: it explicitly identifies failure cases (instruct models, MATH with 3B-Instruct, Qwen) and the large-dataset regime where per-sample adaptation degrades, which increases credibility.
Reasonably thorough experimental matrix (4 method variants × 4 datasets × 2 model sizes) with training dynamics reported and hyperparameter details in the appendix.
weaknesses: Missing key ablations for the central claim of 'adaptivity': no comparison against non-adaptive baselines such as fixed/linear/staged curriculum schedules or random supervision portions. Since prior work (R3, backtracking, Backplay) already shows prefix-conditioned RL helps, it remains unclear how much of the gain comes from the adaptive per-sample update rule versus simply conditioning on prefixes at all. This is the most important missing experiment.

The method requires full ground-truth CoT solutions for every training sample, which sits in tension with the abstract's motivation that dense supervision labels 'become increasingly costly.' The cost profile relative to SFT deserves more careful discussion.

Real-world gains are modest and inconsistent: on MATH, SFT+AdaBack improves over SFT+RL by only ~2 points (9.5 vs 7.4 at 1B), and several comparisons (e.g., GSM8k 3B: AdaBack 73.3 vs SFT+RL 72.7; Tensor-2 3B: AdaBack 49.2 vs SFT+RL 42.7 but SFT+AdaBack drops to 42.2) show mixed results. No error bars, seeds, or significance testing are reported.

R3, the closest related method, is only compared on the synthetic parity task where it is structurally disadvantaged (it requires delimiters); a comparison on GSM8k/MATH, where R3 is applicable, would substantially strengthen the positioning.

Scale and generality are limited: experiments use only LLaMA-3 family models at 1B–3B, and the authors themselves show the method provides no benefit on instruct-tuned or well-covered models, which restricts the practical significance of the 'new capabilities' claim.

The theoretical analysis (Sec. 2.2 and Appendix B) is informal and relies on strong simplifying assumptions (independent parity targets, specific SGD/parity bounds), so the 'separation result' is primarily empirical rather than a theorem; the sample-complexity argument for why AdaBack's exposed-prefix learning dynamics actually work in transformers is heuristic.

Some experimental details raise questions: reporting 'final test accuracy as the average over the last 5 checkpoints' and, in some cases, selecting checkpoints 'with increasing reward' introduces a risk of favorable reporting without clarifying whether this protocol was applied uniformly across all methods.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated problem: the exploration bottleneck of RL for long chain-of-thought reasoning, and clearly frames the 'intermediate regime between SFT and RL' as a research question.
The adaptive update rule is simple, principled (stochastic binary search over supervision ratio), and per-sample, avoiding hand-crafted curriculum staging — a practical design.

The synthetic chain-of-parities task is well designed, with a credible theoretical motivation grounded in parity learning sample complexity (Appendix B), providing a clean separation result between SFT+RL and AdaBack.

The evaluation is reasonably broad: four tasks (MATH, GSM8k, Base-7 GSM8k, Tensor-2 GSM8k), two model sizes, four training variants, plus pass@k analysis supporting the claim of expanded solution space.

The paper is honest about limitations — it explicitly reports settings where AdaBack provides no benefit (instruct-tuned models, MATH with 3B-Instruct) and acknowledges weaknesses in the large-dataset regime.
The new benchmark variants (Base-7, Tensor-2 GSM8k) are a useful contribution for probing generalization beyond pretraining exposure.
weaknesses: Limited novelty over existing work. Revealing partial prefixes of expert demonstrations during RL is well established (reverse curriculum [19], backtracking [43], Backplay [42], R3 [57]); the contribution reduces to a per-sample adaptive schedule over the reveal fraction. Havrilla et al. [26] already tested backtracking curricula and found negligible gains, so the delta must be earned by the adaptivity — the paper does not isolate how much of the gain comes from adaptivity versus simply having any partial-reveal curriculum.

Gains on the real-world benchmarks are small and inconsistent. On GSM8k 3B, SFT+AdaBack (70.7) is worse than SFT+RL (72.7); on Base-7 3B, AdaBack (43.9) is worse than SFT+RL (45.4); on Tensor-2 3B, AdaBack (49.2) beats SFT+RL but SFT+AdaBack (42.2) does not. No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported, so it is hard to judge which differences are significant.

A key contradiction with the motivation: the abstract motivates the method by the cost of dense ground-truth labels, yet AdaBack requires full ground-truth reasoning chains for every training sample — it uses the same supervision as SFT, just revealed partially. The claimed data-efficiency advantage is not demonstrated (no experiments varying the amount of supervision data).

Missing comparisons: R3 is only compared on the synthetic task; there are no results for R3 or other curriculum baselines (e.g., fixed-schedule backtracking, PLR) on MATH/GSM8k. There is also no ablation of the threshold τ, the ρ=0 injection, or the global-average bootstrapping, which are all material hyperparameters of the method.

The headline 'separation result' is on a synthetic task constructed by the authors to have exactly the properties under which AdaBack should succeed; the argument for why degree-2 parities are learnable under prefix conditioning (Appendix B) is informal and relies on simplifying independence assumptions that the authors themselves flag.

The practical impact is limited by the authors' own finding that AdaBack provides no benefit on instruct-tuned or strong pretrained models (MATH 3B-Instruct, Qwen 2.5) — precisely the models used in most current RL-for-reasoning pipelines.

Some experimental choices raise questions: 'in rare cases where performance deteriorated at the end of training, we averaged over the last 5 iterations with increasing reward' is a selection procedure that can bias reported final accuracies. Also, no KL penalty or entropy regularization is used, making the base-model RL comparisons hard to interpret against common practice.

Token-level prefix reveals (k = floor(ρ·m_i)) may cut reasoning mid-step, and the paper provides no analysis of what the revealed prefixes actually contain or whether the model learns genuine reasoning versus memorizing completions; qualitative examples are absent.

No code release or sufficient implementation detail (e.g., how rewards feed the interval update within a GRPO batch with 8 rollouts per sample, handling of non-stationarity across epochs) is provided, weakening reproducibility.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: the paper identifies an intermediate regime between SFT and RL and directly tests whether adaptive partial supervision can enable learning where both fail, rather than merely improving efficiency.

The core method (AdaBack) is simple, elegant, and practically sensible: a per-sample stochastic binary search over the supervision ratio driven by the average reward across GRPO rollouts, requiring only a single threshold and no handcrafted curriculum stages or step delimiters.

The synthetic chain-of-parities task provides a genuine separation result: SFT, RL, and SFT+RL all fail while AdaBack succeeds, and the parity-learning-complexity argument in Appendix B gives an informed (if informal) theoretical rationale for why the curriculum helps.

Thoughtful evaluation design: the Base-7 and Tensor-2 GSM8k variants are useful probes for pretraining contamination and longer-horizon reasoning; the pass@k analysis directly engages the 'RL only reweights existing capabilities' hypothesis (Yue et al.) and provides evidence that AdaBack expands the solution space, especially without SFT.

The paper is unusually candid about limitations: it explicitly reports the failure case (MATH with 3B-Instruct, Qwen 2.5), discusses the large-dataset regime where per-sample adaptation degrades, and shows cases where AdaBack underperforms SFT+RL (e.g., GSM8k 3B, Tensor-2 3B), which increases credibility.
Compute budget and RL setup details (80k A100 GPU hours, GRPO, 8 rollouts, hyperparameters) are reported, aiding reproducibility assessment.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than groundbreaking. Revealing prefixes of expert demonstrations and gradually shifting the reveal point backward exists in prior work (Salimans & Chen's backtracking, Backplay, Florensa's reverse curriculum, R3). The delta is essentially per-sample adaptivity via reward-thresholded binary search plus token-level (rather than step-delimited) slicing, which is an incremental refinement of a known idea.

AdaBack still requires full gold rationales for every training sample, which weakens the abstract's framing that SFT's weakness is the cost of dense ground-truth labels; the supervision cost of AdaBack is the same as SFT. The advantage is purely in training dynamics/exploration, and the paper would be clearer on this point.

The theoretical separation argument (Appendix B) relies on simplifying assumptions (independent parity targets, known SQ/SGD sample-complexity bounds carried over to transformers) and is acknowledged as heuristic; no formal theorem is provided for the claimed separation.

Table 1 results are inconsistent across settings and modest on the cleanest benchmarks: on MATH the gains are small (9.1 vs 7.4 at 1B), and SFT+AdaBack underperforms SFT+RL on GSM8k-3B (70.7 vs 72.7) and Tensor-2-3B (42.2 vs 42.7). No error bars, seed variance, or significance tests are reported, so several claimed improvements may not be robust.

Baselines are limited to GRPO and SFT+GRPO. The main curriculum competitor (R3) is compared only on the synthetic task; there is no comparison on real benchmarks against other curricula (e.g., a fixed annealing schedule of the reveal ratio, difficulty-based problem ordering), which is needed to isolate the value of the adaptive per-sample mechanism vs. curriculum learning in general.

The method introduces several additional heuristics (reward threshold τ, 10% ρ=0 injection, format reward, global EMA bootstrapping) with no ablations or sensitivity analysis; it is unclear how much of the gain depends on these choices.

The 'new reasoning capabilities' claim, while supported by pass@k gains, is somewhat overclaimed given the small models, the reliance on gold prefixes for training, and the fact that the strongest evidence comes from the authors' own synthetic construction and their new GSM8k variants rather than standard benchmarks.
No code release is mentioned, which—combined with multiple undocumented implementation choices—affects reproducibility.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: probing the underexplored regime between full SFT supervision and sparse-reward RL, with adaptive per-sample partial-supervision scheduling (AdaBack) as a concrete, simple instantiation.

The synthetic chain-of-parities task is a nice, theory-informed construction (connected to parity/curriculum learning literature, e.g., Abbe et al.) that provides an interpretable separation result: AdaBack learns a task where SFT, RL, and SFT+RL all fail, with a plausible explanation (reducing degree-3 to degree-2 parity via revealed prefixes).

Comprehensive experimental design: four variants (Base+RL, SFT+RL, AdaBack, SFT+AdaBack) across three benchmarks plus two thoughtful new out-of-distribution GSM8k variants (Base-7 and Tensor-2) specifically designed to test generalization beyond pretraining exposure.

Direct, well-controlled comparison with R3 using identical ground-truth solutions and reward functions, isolating the curriculum mechanism; the paper honestly reports that R3 wins on GSM8k and analyzes why (segmentation brittleness vs. per-sample adaptivity).

Thorough supporting analyses: pass@k evaluation testing whether AdaBack expands the solution distribution (contra Yue et al. 2025), sensitivity analysis over the threshold τ showing robustness, identification and analysis of failure cases (MATH with 3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-1.5B), and detailed appendices with hyperparameters and compute budget (~80k A100 hours).
Honest limitations section, including the large-dataset regime where per-sample statistics degrade, and cases where AdaBack provides no benefit.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: revealing solution prefixes and gradually shifting the start point backward is well-established (Salimans & Chen 2018, Backplay, Florensa et al. 2017, R3). The core contribution is essentially making this scheduling per-sample and reward-driven—a heuristic update rule (interval halving on ρ) that is simple and plausible but not theoretically grounded; the convergence/optimality of the stochastic binary search over ρ is not analyzed.

Real-world gains are modest and inconsistent: on standard benchmarks the improvements over SFT+RL are often within 1-3 points (e.g., DeepScaleR 1B: 7.1→9.0; MATH 3B: 17.7→19.1), and R3 outperforms AdaBack on GSM8k for both model sizes. No error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported for Table 1, so the significance of these small gaps is unclear given acknowledged RL training variance.

A potential train/test mismatch is inherent to the approach: training conditions on gold-solution prefixes while evaluation requires fully self-generated chains. The ρ=0 injection trick (10% of the time) mitigates this but is a patch; the paper does not analyze how much of the gain comes from the model implicitly copying/format-attuning to revealed gold content rather than learning to explore, particularly on Base-7/Tensor-2 where memorization-style gains are plausible.

The separation 'result' is purely empirical; the Appendix B argument relies on simplifying assumptions (independent parity targets, SQ lower bounds applied heuristically to SGD-trained transformers) and the paper concedes exact training dynamics are not explored.

Concern about evaluation fairness: final scores are averaged over the last 5 checkpoints, and in 'rare cases' where performance deteriorated, the authors select the last 5 iterations with increasing reward—this cherry-picking criterion is not clearly defined and could favor AdaBack.
No code or artifact release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a method with several non-trivial implementation details (EMA bootstrapping, ρ=0 injection, format rewards).

Key claimed strengths (advantage on long-horizon, heterogeneous tasks) are extrapolated rather than demonstrated: the real datasets used 'still contain only a few reasoning steps,' so the main motivating scenario for per-sample adaptivity over R3-style segmentation remains untested on real data.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely question—the exploration bottleneck in RL for LLM reasoning—and frames the 'partial supervision regime' between SFT and RL clearly.

The chain-of-parities synthetic task with a latent parity structure is a nice probe, and the empirical separation (AdaBack succeeds where SFT, RL, and SFT+RL fail) is a well-motivated demonstration, supported by a reasonable informal argument connecting prefix reveals to lower parity degree.

The evaluation is broad: four method variants, two model sizes, three standard benchmarks plus two constructed GSM8k variants, a comparison with the closest prior method (R3), pass@k analysis, ablations over the threshold τ, and honest reporting of failure cases (instruct models, saturated datasets).

The method is simple and hyperparameter-light, with robustness to τ empirically demonstrated, and the per-sample (rather than dataset-level) curriculum is a genuine design distinction from R3 and batch-level curricula.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core idea—training on progressively longer completions of expert solutions starting from near the goal—is well established (Salimans & Chen 2018; Florensa et al. 2017; Backplay; R3). The contribution reduces to making the reveal length per-sample adaptive via a stochastic binary search on the reward signal, which is an incremental modification of reverse-curriculum RL.

Real-world gains are modest and mixed. In Table 1, AdaBack improves 1B results but several 3B settings show no gain or regression (e.g., GSM8k 3B: SFT+RL 72.7 vs SFT+AdaBack 70.7; Base+RL GSM8k 3B already reaches 63.7). In the direct R3 comparison (Table 2), R3 wins on GSM8k for both model sizes, and AdaBack's advantage on MATH (9.1 vs 7.8, 19.1 vs 19.2) is within typical RL run-to-run variance. The headline claim of 'genuinely new reasoning capabilities' is not strongly supported on real tasks.

No statistical rigor: no multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite acknowledging 'the inherent variance of RL post-training.' Reporting the average of the last 5 checkpoints, with special handling 'in rare cases where performance deteriorated' (averaging over the last 5 iterations with increasing reward), introduces a selective-reporting concern.

The theoretical motivation (sample complexity of degree-3 vs degree-2 parities, SQ lower bounds) is heuristic; Appendix B concedes it rests on strong simplifying assumptions (independent parity targets, architecture-dependent dynamics) and no actual learning-theoretic result is proven for AdaBack.

Absolute performance levels are low (DeepScaleR 6–12%, MATH 6–20% with Llama-3 base models), making it hard to assess whether these conclusions transfer to settings where RL is actually competitive; the paper also concedes no benefit on instruct/modern reasoning models, which substantially narrows practical relevance.
The synthetic-task comparison to R3 (Fig. 2) is on AdaBack's most favorable terrain and the >20x efficiency claim is not substantiated on any real benchmark.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('he superior performance', 'sequences learning tasks'), dense caption/figure design, and no mention of code release, which weakens reproducibility for a method whose details (EMA bootstrapping, ρ=0 injection, delimiter/format handling) matter.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and important question: whether partial (rationale-prefix) supervision can enable learning regimes that neither SFT nor RL can reach, and frames it clearly as an intermediate regime between SFT and RL.

AdaBack is simple, well-specified, and genuinely per-sample: the stochastic binary search over supervision ratios driven by GRPO rollout rewards is elegant, avoids hand-crafted curriculum stages, and is shown to be robust to the main hyperparameter τ (Appendix C/D ablations).

The chain-of-parities synthetic task provides a clean separation result, and the accompanying theoretical discussion (Appendix B, grounding in parity sample-complexity results) explains why SFT, RL, and SFT+RL fail while AdaBack succeeds — this is more than an empirical engineering paper.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: four training variants (base/GRPO, SFT/GRPO, AdaBack, SFT+AdaBack), two model sizes, three math benchmarks plus two out-of-distribution GSM8k variants (Base-7, Tensor-2), a direct comparison with the closest prior method (R3) that isolates the curriculum mechanism, and a pass@k analysis supporting the claim that AdaBack expands rather than reweights the solution distribution.

The paper is commendably honest about failure cases (instruct/saturated models) and limitations (large-dataset regime, reliance on ground-truth CoT), and positions itself carefully against reverse-curriculum, backtracking, and batch-level curriculum work.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the core idea — revealing solution prefixes and progressively reducing supervision — is well established (reverse curriculum in RL: Salimans & Chen 2018, Florensa et al. 2017, Backplay; R3 in LLM reasoning). The contribution is essentially per-sample adaptivity of an existing curriculum mechanism, which is an incremental delta over R3.

Gains on real-world benchmarks are small and inconsistent with the headline framing. Many Table 1 improvements are within 1–3 points (e.g., GSM8k 3B: 73.3 vs 72.7 SFT+RL), and Table 2 shows R3 outperforms AdaBack on GSM8k for both sizes and roughly ties on MATH-3B. Given the well-documented high variance of RL post-training, no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported, so the statistical significance of the claimed improvements is unclear.

The separation claim (tasks where SFT+RL fails but AdaBack succeeds) is demonstrated only on a small synthetic parity task with one model (Llama 3.2 1B, L=16, n=1024). The generality of this result to realistic long-horizon reasoning is conjectured but not shown, and the authors themselves concede real datasets used have 'only a few reasoning steps.'

There are apparent inconsistencies between Table 1 and Table 2 (e.g., GSM8k 3B: AdaBack base 73.3 in Table 1, but 73.3/74.2 comparisons in Table 2 make the R3 comparison read as AdaBack losing on its own headline setting), and the text's explanation for this (segmentation brittleness, dataset heterogeneity) is post-hoc and not experimentally validated.

Method applicability is limited by its dependence on ground-truth chain-of-thought rationales for every training sample — precisely the resource the introduction says is scarce in specialized domains. The absolute accuracies reported (e.g., DeepScaleR at 9–12%) are also low, weakening practical impact claims relative to standard pipelines.

Key experimental details that affect reproducibility and fairness are only partially described in the main text (e.g., SFT data/recipe, dataset sizes per task, how prefix reveals interact with tokenization/format tokens), and several claims (e.g., 'training is not sensitive to τ') are supported on only one model–dataset combination.
